overview: Wall Street's tech-led slide deepened after Alphabet reported a revenue miss that revived worries about the cost of AI spending, while oil stayed above $100 a barrel. ECB President Christine Lagarde said she will step down early, setting off a scramble over her successor, and the ECB held rates but flagged a possible December hike. Brazil re-elected Lula, Serbia's Student List won a parliamentary majority, and a high-speed train collision in Spain killed at least 69 people, per Wikipedia's news summary. In the US, the midterm elections are days away.

stories.headline: Alaska governor orders probe as DOJ widens inquiry into second 'Dan Sullivan' on Senate ballot
stories.summary: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into whether people tied to Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign helped put a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the Senate ballot against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Peltola says she knew nothing about it. The Justice Department is reported to be escalating its own probe, and Dunleavy has said certification of the race could be 'stopped or changed'.
stories.why_it_matters: A close Senate race that could help decide control of the chamber may now hinge on how votes for two same-named candidates are counted and when results are certified. Alaska voters could face delays or court fights over the outcome.
stories.background: Alaska's Senate race this year pits incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, plus other candidates. A separate man named Daniel Sullivan qualified for the ballot over the summer, which Republicans say was meant to confuse voters. Sullivan's allies tried to have the second candidate removed and did not succeed. The Justice Department has also sued Alaska over how votes for the second Sullivan should be handled at certification, and Peltola's campaign has asked a judge to dismiss that suit. Democrats and Peltola's campaign deny any scheme.

facts.text: CBS News reported that Alaska's governor ordered a probe after a report alleged people aligned with Peltola's campaign helped recruit the second Dan Sullivan; Peltola denied the allegations.
Peltola said she 'knew nothing about' the other Dan Sullivan, according to CBS News and the Associated Press.
ABC News reported that the Justice Department had escalated its investigation, and Fox News described it as an intensifying criminal probe.

Gov. Dunleavy told NewsNation the state grew suspicious in May and June after an email asked to list a newcomer on the ballot as 'Daniel S. Sullivan', and said certification could be 'stopped or changed'.
The Washington Examiner reported that Alaska's Republican-run elections office could decline to certify the race, which would leave the outcome in limbo.
The Justice Department has sued Alaska asking it to hold off certifying any result affected by voter confusion; Peltola and the state Democratic Party moved to intervene in the suit.

stories.headline: Judge refuses DOJ bid to set aside California ballots as grand jury subpoenas go out
stories.summary: A federal judge in California rejected a Justice Department request to separate mail ballots from about 20,000 people it alleges are noncitizens. A day later the department issued grand jury subpoenas to California election officials in a criminal probe.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling means those ballots are processed normally ahead of the midterms, while the subpoenas show the dispute over California's voter rolls is widening beyond the courtroom.
stories.background: The Trump administration's Justice Department sued California over its voter rolls, saying about 20,000 registrants may not be citizens. California and Los Angeles County say the federal government has not shown how it built the list and that it may be inaccurate. U.S. District Judge David Carter has been hearing the case and has floated appointing a special master to review the claims.

facts.text: U.S. District Judge David Carter on Wednesday denied the administration's request to segregate mail ballots from roughly 20,000 people it alleges are noncitizens.
Carter wrote that registered voters 'must not be deprived of a core right merely because of unfounded allegations' from a process 'rife with uncertainty and errors'.
PBS reported the judge warned that segregating the ballots would 'wreak havoc' on the election.
The Justice Department then issued grand jury subpoenas to California local election officials, including in Los Angeles, as part of a criminal investigation.

The state argued that returned ballots are already separated from identifying envelopes and that more than 3 million had been returned; Carter said a special master could finish review before the Dec. 11 certification deadline.

stories.headline: Israel's election ends without a majority for either bloc as Netanyahu's party alleges fraud
stories.summary: Final results from Israel's general election show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc ahead but eight seats short of a majority, with Gadi Eisenkot's bloc behind and Arab-led parties holding the balance. Netanyahu's Likud has alleged, without providing evidence, that the vote was tainted by fraud and foreign involvement; police and other officials have rejected the claims. Weeks of coalition talks, or another election, now lie ahead.
stories.why_it_matters: Who governs Israel shapes the war and ceasefire diplomacy, regional security and oil-market nerves, and the unresolved result means policy decisions may stall for weeks. The fraud claims also raise questions about trust in the vote itself.
stories.background: Israel elects a 120-seat Knesset and a government needs 61 seats, which almost always requires a coalition of several parties. This was the country's first national election since Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack. Netanyahu has led the government for most of the past two decades and leads a coalition of right-wing, religious and far-right parties. His main rival this time is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who leads the Yashar party. Arab-led parties, which usually sit outside coalitions, won their largest combined showing, putting them in a position to influence what government can form.

facts.text: Final results showed Netanyahu's coalition won the most seats but fell eight short of a parliamentary majority.
The Times of Israel reported the seat split as 53 for Netanyahu's bloc, 48 for Eisenkot's bloc and 19 for Arab parties.
NBC News reported that Arab minority-led parties won a combined 19 seats in a race with record turnout among Arab citizens of Israel.
Likud alleged on Thursday, without providing evidence, that Arab parties' gains were driven in part by voter fraud.
President Isaac Herzog called for an investigation of the fraud allegations while cautioning against stigmatizing the whole Arab Israeli community.
Qatar called accusations of election interference "ridiculous and dangerous"; the Guardian reported Israeli police and opposition parties also dismissed Netanyahu's claim.
Polymarket said it is investigating suspicious trades placed shortly before polls closed, betting on Netanyahu doing better than his opponent, the WSJ reported.

stories.headline: Spain's second deadly high-speed train crash in a year raises questions about signaling and human error
stories.summary: Two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on Wednesday, and the toll has risen to 69 dead according to France 24. Leaked audio between a control centre and train drivers appears to show one train was cleared to move while another had stalled on the track. Spain, heading toward national elections, is asking whether its rail system is too old or too prone to human error.
stories.why_it_matters: Millions of people in Spain and visitors rely on its high-speed rail, and the crash puts the safety of the network and the oversight of its operators in question.
stories.background: Spain built one of the world's largest high-speed rail networks and has long promoted it as a model. Services are run by the state operator Renfe and private competitors such as Iryo, with the infrastructure managed by the state company Adif. This is the country's second major rail disaster this year. Rail safety has become a campaign issue ahead of the national election.

facts.text: The toll from Spain's second high-speed collision this year rose to 69, France 24 reported, with scores injured.
Recordings between a control centre and train drivers appear to show one train was given clearance to move although another had stalled on the track, the BBC reported.
NBC News also reported new audio that appears to reveal the moments leading up to the crash.
The crash is the country's second major rail disaster in a year, and rail safety has become an election campaign issue.
Reports put the collision near Urda station in Toledo province, south of Madrid.

stories.headline: Iran says tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz as oil prices rise
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said several oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, saying the ships had switched off navigation systems and ignored warnings. A separate tanker was attacked by a small boat carrying explosive devices, and oil prices rose. Iran also disputes a US claim that shipping lanes had been cleared.
stories.why_it_matters: A large share of the world's oil passes through the strait, so attacks there can push up fuel prices and shipping costs for consumers. Oil spills are also reaching Gulf beaches.
stories.background: The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow passage at the mouth of the Persian Gulf through which much of the world's oil is shipped. Iran and the United States are in a conflict that has disrupted shipping there for months. US Central Command said in August that international shipping lanes had been cleared of mines, which Iran's navy rejected. Qatar is among the mediators trying to end the war.

CBS News reported a tanker was also struck by a projectile in the strait Thursday night.
The Financial Times reported oil from the tanker attacks has washed up on UAE beaches and that Tehran has stepped up strikes on vessels over the past month.

stories.headline: Binance halts withdrawals after what may be the largest crypto hack on record
stories.summary: Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, suspended deposits and withdrawals after a suspected security breach, with reports putting the losses at $5.7 billion to $6.3 billion. Binance said about $3 billion in assets has been frozen, with stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether freezing related assets. Two analytics firms have linked the theft to a North Korean hacking unit; Binance plans to reopen within days.
stories.why_it_matters: Millions of people hold funds on exchanges like Binance, and a freeze or loss could affect their access to money and shake crypto prices.
stories.background: Binance is the largest cryptocurrency exchange by volume, where users trade and store digital assets. Hackers have repeatedly targeted exchanges, and North Korean groups have been blamed for some of the largest thefts. Stablecoin issuers such as Circle and Tether can freeze tokens, which is one way stolen funds can be contained. The hack follows a wave of other high-profile cyberattacks, Axios reported.

facts.text: Binance said on Thursday it had frozen about $3 billion in crypto assets while investigating a potential breach, with Circle and Tether freezing related assets.
Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while it conducts security checks.
Two analytics firms attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor, the BBC reported.
The FT reported that Binance said an engineer's laptop was compromised.
MarketWatch reported Binance vowed to be back up within a couple of days.

Upwards of $5.7 billion drained from wallets, per Axios.

stories.headline: Russian drone strike on Dnipro train station kills at least 14; Ukraine reportedly resumes refinery strikes
stories.summary: A Russian drone strike hit trains at a station in Dnipro, killing at least 14 people, Ukrainian officials said. Separately, the WSJ reported that Ukraine had paused strikes on Russian oil refineries after pressure from President Trump, and then reported a new strike on a refinery that ended the pause. Coverage of the refinery story comes from center-rated outlets only.
stories.why_it_matters: The war continues to kill civilians far from the front, and US pressure over Russian oil facilities touches fuel markets and the pace of peace efforts.
stories.background: Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and regularly strikes Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles. Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries to reduce Moscow's fuel supply and revenue. President Trump has pressed both sides toward a settlement. A rare local ceasefire around the occupied town of Oleshky was also in place, the NYT reported.

Russian attacks across Ukraine killed 27 and injured 127 over the past day, the Kyiv Independent reported.
CBS reported a local truce around Oleshky, credited to Melania Trump, is bringing some hope.

stories.headline: North Korea fires missiles and tests attack drones as Kim calls for drone dominance
stories.summary: North Korea fired a missile barrage toward the sea, and state media reported tests of attack drones, cruise missiles and rocket launchers as Kim Jong Un urged faster drone and AI development. South Korea says it will respond firmly to North Korean border breaches. Pyongyang has denounced US-South Korean air defence drills.
stories.why_it_matters: Rising tension on the Korean peninsula affects the safety of people in the region and can disrupt flights, shipping and markets.
stories.background: North Korea has conducted repeated weapons tests this month, the Washington Times counted a third barrage. Tensions with South Korea rose after blasts on September 21 along the border. Seoul blames mines it says North Korea planted south of the demarcation line, and Pyongyang denies this. The US and South Korea hold regular joint military drills that the North condemns.

stories.headline: US seizes crypto in Kenya tied to alleged 'ghost student' financial aid fraud
stories.summary: US authorities seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency in Kenya linked to a scheme in which stolen identities were allegedly used to claim US student aid, with Kenyans among those charged. The Justice Department described it as its first international seizure of its kind in Kenya. Coverage comes from center and right outlets only, with no lean-left outlets in the digest.
stories.why_it_matters: The case shows how fraud against US federal aid is being pursued across borders, and it implicates ordinary people whose identities were used.
stories.background: 'Ghost students' are fake or stolen identities enrolled in colleges so that someone can collect federal student aid. The US Justice Department has been prosecuting such schemes. In this case, Kenyan nationals are among those charged, and Kenyan investigators helped with the seizure, the US Embassy said. A Kenyan court has also heard a dispute over funds in a related probe.

stories.headline: Tech stocks slide as Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft results renew doubts about AI spending
stories.summary: US tech shares fell on Thursday after Alphabet reported revenue below expectations, and the selloff extended into Friday after Amazon and Intel results. Outlets tie the drop to investor doubts about whether huge AI spending will pay off. Investors moved into Treasuries, pushing yields to multiweek lows, per the Wall Street Journal.
stories.why_it_matters: Big tech stocks make up a large share of index funds and retirement accounts, so a sustained slide can show up in 401(k) balances. The same spending worries also bear on borrowing costs, since Microsoft is planning a large bond sale.
stories.background: The biggest US technology companies have been spending heavily on data centers and chips to build artificial-intelligence services, and their shares drove the S&P 500 to repeated record highs this year. Each quarter, investors check whether that spending is producing matching growth in cloud, search and advertising revenue. Alphabet (Google's parent), Microsoft and Amazon all reported quarterly results this week. When results or spending plans disappoint, investors tend to sell the sector and buy safer assets such as US Treasury bonds.

facts.text: The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.4% on Thursday after Alphabet and Microsoft reported, according to the Financial Times.

The Wall Street Journal and the Associated Press both described Alphabet's share drop as historic; the Journal said a revenue shortfall caused one of the largest one-session market-value losses on record for a single company.
CNBC reported that Alphabet's revenue from its core business came in below analyst estimates.

Amazon's cloud unit AWS grew revenue 39%, per CNBC; Reuters called it the fastest cloud growth in five years, yet Amazon shares fell as AI spending outweighed it, and the AP said the company gave a cautious outlook.
Reuters, citing sources, reported Microsoft expects to raise $25 billion in a US bond sale.
On Friday the selloff deepened after Amazon and Intel results, and Treasury yields fell to multiweek lows as investors sought safety, per the Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg.
The New York Times reported the S&P 500 was still on track for a small gain for October.

stories.headline: US economy grew 3.4% in third quarter as September inflation picked up
stories.summary: The government's first estimate showed US output grew at a 3.4% annual pace in July through September, the fastest in a year, led by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Reuters and Fox Business reported the Fed's preferred inflation gauge rose in September. Mortgage rates dipped to 7.24%, per Freddie Mac.
stories.why_it_matters: Strong growth with rising prices makes it harder for the Fed to cut rates, which keeps mortgage and loan costs high. The mortgage rate is still above 7%, so home buying stays expensive even after the dip.
stories.background: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the broadest measure of the size of the US economy, and the quarterly figure shows how fast it is growing. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index is the inflation measure the Federal Reserve targets when it sets interest rates. The Fed weighs growth against inflation: faster growth and prices tend to argue against lowering rates. The data arrives less than a week before the midterm elections, where views of the economy are a campaign issue.

facts.text: US GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, per the Associated Press, Reuters and CNBC, which described it as better than expected.
The New York Times said it was the fastest pace in a year and contrasted it with the poor marks many voters give the economy.
Reuters reported US inflation heated up in September while consumer spending rose; Fox Business said the Fed's preferred gauge rose.
CNBC said economists in a Dow Jones survey had expected the PCE price index to rise 0.5% in September, a 3.7% annual rate.
Freddie Mac said the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell to 7.24% from 7.32% a week earlier, the lowest in more than a month.

stories.headline: ECB president Lagarde to step down early as bank holds rates
stories.summary: Christine Lagarde said she will leave the European Central Bank around February, about nine months before her term ends. Her announcement came the same day the ECB left interest rates unchanged. Reuters reported, citing sources, that governors see a December rate hike as likely.
stories.why_it_matters: The ECB sets interest rates for the euro-area countries, so its next leader will influence loan costs and the euro's value, which affect travel costs and global markets. Choosing a successor may become a contest among Europe's largest countries.
stories.background: Lagarde, a former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund, has led the ECB since 2019 on an eight-year term. The bank's president is chosen by EU leaders. The Associated Press said her early exit lets them pick a successor before France's presidential election. France 24 reported her departure will fuel speculation about her future plans, and the Guardian said she may be a candidate to run the World Economic Forum.

facts.text: Lagarde said she will resign early, with the New York Times reporting a planned February departure and the Guardian saying nine months before her term ends.
France 24 reported she wants more "freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy."
The ECB kept interest rates unchanged on Thursday, and the euro and bond yields fell, per Reuters.

Reuters, citing sources, said ECB governors see a December rate hike as likely, followed by a pause; a second Reuters story said the ECB flagged a December hike but expects higher yields to weigh on growth.
European shares closed at a seven-week high after the ECB pause and the Lagarde news, per Reuters.
The Wall Street Journal reported Europe's largest countries are already jockeying over her successor.

stories.headline: BP and Chevron post strong profits on refining margins
stories.summary: BP reported third-quarter profit of about $8.5 billion, and Chevron beat analyst expectations, with both pointing to strong refining margins. Sinopec in China also reported higher profit. Oil prices rose on Thursday and Friday.
stories.why_it_matters: Strong refining margins can mean higher prices for diesel and other fuels, which feed into shipping and grocery costs. Energy stocks are also one of the few areas rising while tech falls.
stories.background: Refining margins are the gap between what refiners pay for crude oil and what they earn selling fuels like diesel and gasoline. They rise when supply of those fuels is tight. CNBC attributed this quarter's squeeze to attacks by Ukraine and Iran on refineries in Russia and the Middle East. Bloomberg said BP is using the windfall to speed up efforts to repair its balance sheet and pay down debt.

facts.text: BP's third-quarter profit nearly quadrupled to $8.5 billion, according to CNBC, and Bloomberg said it was the highest in 18 years.
Chevron beat earnings expectations as refining profits rose on high diesel prices, per CNBC, which linked diesel prices to attacks on refineries in Russia and the Middle East.

stories.headline: FDNY blames e-bike battery for Bronx fire that killed an 11-year-old
stories.summary: The FDNY said a lithium-ion battery in an e-bike started a fire in the Bronx that killed 11-year-old Zion Maine and injured four relatives. Neighbors held a vigil at the Patterson Houses in Mott Haven, and THE CITY reported that e-bike battery fires are rising in NYCHA housing.
stories.why_it_matters: Residents of public and older apartment buildings face fire risk from charging e-bikes indoors, and the city has no NYCHA-wide ban in place according to THE CITY's reporting of the 2023 debate.
stories.background: Lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes and scooters have been a growing fire hazard in New York for several years, especially in apartments. In 2023, after fatal fires in NYCHA apartments, the housing authority considered banning the devices outright, but opposition emerged from those who rely on them, THE CITY reported. This week's fire killed a boy on Wednesday. FDNY officials said the batteries have caused more than 400 fires across the city this year.

stories.headline: Mamdani and Menin name new racial equity commission chair, but not until August 2027
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Council Speaker Julie Menin formally appointed Christopher Alexander to lead the city's independent racial equity watchdog starting in August 2027. The timing reflects an agreement reached after Council members objected to replacing current chair Linda Tigani sooner. Only amNY's report is in the digest.
stories.why_it_matters: The commission reviews how city agencies treat racial equity, so who leads it and when shapes how independent that oversight is. The dispute shows the mayor and Council negotiating over appointments.
stories.background: The Commission on Racial Equity is an independent city body. Mamdani had moved to replace its chair, Linda Tigani, who had criticized the administration's handling of the city's first racial equity plan, according to reports that surfaced in October. Council members, including supporters who rallied at City Hall, pushed back. TheGrio reported Alexander, who leads the NAACP New York State Conference, as the mayor's pick.

stories.headline: NYC public school enrollment keeps falling
stories.summary: The Daily News reported that K-12 enrollment in the city fell 19% over a decade, raising concerns about resources. The New York Post separately reported the decline is occurring even as spending rises.
stories.why_it_matters: Fewer students affect school budgets, staffing and building use, and fuels debate over school closures and per-pupil spending.
stories.background: New York City public school enrollment has been falling. Policymakers have argued over whether to cut class sizes or consolidate schools as rolls shrink. Mayor Mamdani's administration and the Department of Education manage the system.

facts.text: The Daily News reported that K-12 enrollment in NYC fell 19% over a decade.
The Post reported enrollment is dropping while spending rises.

stories.headline: Riders Alliance launches campaign for faster, free buses
stories.summary: Riders Alliance has begun a campaign using union and tenant organizing tactics to build a base of bus riders behind faster and free bus service, amNY reported. The group calls the city's bus system the nation's slowest.
stories.why_it_matters: Bus speed and fares affect millions of daily riders, and the campaign is aimed at pressure on city and state officials. Only amNY's report is in the digest.
stories.background: Riders Alliance is a transit advocacy group that has pushed for bus lanes, faster service and fare relief. Fare-free buses were a central promise of Mayor Mamdani's campaign. Paying for them and speeding service would require action by the city and the MTA, which is state-controlled.

facts.text: Riders Alliance launched a campaign called 'Fix the Bus' to organize riders behind faster, free bus service, using tactics common in labor and tenant organizing.

markets.summary: US tech stocks sold off as the market weakened: the Nasdaq Composite lost 1.38% and the Dow slipped 0.25%, per the latest figures. Reuters and AP attributed the move to Alphabet's revenue miss, which revived concern about how much companies are spending on AI. Oil remains elevated, with WTI near $103 and Brent above $123, which keeps inflation pressure in view: the latest CPI reading is 3.72% year over year. The 10-year Treasury yield is 5.05%, and the average 30-year mortgage rate is 7.24%, down 8 basis points on the day. Bitcoin fell about 4%.

concept.explanation: Capex is money a company spends on long-lasting assets such as data centers, chips and factories, rather than on day-to-day costs. It rises when executives expect demand to grow, and investors watch it closely: heavy spending can pay off later but cuts into profit now, which is why AI spending plans can move a stock. It reaches your wallet through your retirement account, since big tech stocks make up a large part of popular index funds, and through the jobs and electricity demand that new data centers bring.
